description:
DESC

We are 3rd-year CSE students at New Horizon College of Engineering, Bengaluru, taking on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, using satellite soil moisture, rainfall and vegetation data to help farmers adapt to climate change. We bring Python, ML, data analysis and React web development. We are looking for a frontend/UI developer (maps, dashboards), a data/GIS specialist and a design/pitch lead. We are committed, organised and focused on delivering a complete, competitive solution.
summary:
Field Shift is an interactive 3D map that shows how climate change will reshape what South India's farms can grow. It scores 131 districts across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Goa for paddy, ragi and maize, comparing today's climate (2001–2020) with 2041–2060 under two emission scenarios, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5.

The scores come from NASA's NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 downscaled climate projections, checked against NASA POWER observations (r = 0.94). MODIS greenness and land surface temperature show what each district's fields have done over the last 20 years. A timelapse slider and a before/after swipe let anyone watch the shift happen. Clicking a district gives a plain-language plan: the best crop now and in 2050, how many weeks sowing should move as the monsoon shifts, and how much extra water each crop would need.

Climate projections rarely reach the people deciding what to plant. Field Shift turns NASA data into one map that a farmer, extension officer or planner can read in a minute.
details:
What it does

Field Shift scores how well each of 131 South Indian districts suits paddy, ragi and maize, today (2001–2020) and in 2050 (2041–2060), under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. Districts are drawn as 3D columns whose height and colour show suitability. A slider animates the change from today to 2050, a swipe view compares the two side by side, and a guided story walks through the key findings.

How it works

The score is a transparent rule: 100 × the lower of a temperature factor and a rainfall factor. Each factor is 1 inside the crop's optimal range (FAO ECOCROP) and falls to 0 at its limits. Climate is the mean of five NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models (ACCESS-CM2, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MRI-ESM2-0, NorESM2-MM) over the June–October kharif season, averaged to districts. We also derive monsoon onset from daily rainfall. NASA POWER rainfall validates the model baseline (r = 0.94). MODIS NDVI and land surface temperature, masked to cropland with ESA WorldCover, provide each district's observed 20-year record.

Benefits and impact

Each district gets an adaptation plan: the best crop now and in 2050, whether to switch crops, how many weeks sowing should move, and the water gap per crop in mm. Headline findings: kharif rainfall rises about 10–15% and temperature about 1.0–1.4 °C by 2050. Paddy gains on the wet coast (Thiruvananthapuram 30 → 68). Maize opens up in the dry interior (Anantapur 36 → 95). Ragi loses suitability in up to 65 of 131 districts.

Tools

Python (numpy, shapely, netCDF4, requests) for the data pipeline. FastAPI for an optional API. Next.js 14, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, deck.gl and Tailwind for the frontend. Hosted on Vercel. Every number is precomputed into static files, so the site is fast and works without a backend.

Creativity

The NASA data is shown as a 3D landscape that rises and falls as you scrub through time. Every number in the app links back to its source dataset.

What we considered

Honesty about limits. The model covers rain-fed crops in the kharif season only, so irrigated districts and the north-east monsoon (important in Tamil Nadu) are under-represented. District averages hide local variation. Results are scenarios, not forecasts, and model spread is shown for every district.
